topics.title: Ovulation Induction & OHSS
topics.frontClue: Measure follicles, trigger near 18 to 20 mm, watch for huge ovaries and ascites
topics.corePiece: Ovulation induction uses drugs such as letrozole, clomiphene or injectable gonadotropins. A baseline transvaginal scan early in the cycle (about day 2 or 3) checks for residual cysts and records the antral follicle count (follicles about 2 to 10 mm). Serial scans measure each growing follicle and record endometrial thickness and pattern. An hCG or GnRH-agonist trigger is usually given when lead follicles reach about 18 to 20 mm for timed intercourse or insemination, or when several follicles reach about 17 to 18 mm in IVF. A trilaminar endometrium of about 7 mm or more is favorable. Too many mature follicles may lead to cycle cancellation to prevent multiple pregnancy and ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome (OHSS). OHSS usually follows the trigger or early pregnancy, which raises hCG. It produces enlarged ovaries, often 5 to 10 cm or more, filled with many large cysts (spoke-wheel appearance), plus ascites, pleural effusion, hemoconcentration, oliguria and thrombosis risk. Risk factors include PCOS, young age, high antral follicle count and high estradiol. Enlarged ovaries can torse.
topics.whyLock: Monitoring is about balance: enough follicles to achieve pregnancy, not so many that the patient risks multiples or OHSS. Exams ask what to measure (follicle size and count, endometrium), when to trigger, and what OHSS looks like. A trap is misreading the large stimulated cysts as malignant multilocular masses; the history is decisive. Remember the fluid shifts: scan the abdomen and chest for ascites and effusions. Pregnancy prolongs OHSS because hCG keeps stimulating the ovaries, and heterotopic pregnancy risk is higher in these patients.

topics.title: Sonohysterography
topics.frontClue: Early proliferative phase, saline through a catheter, no pregnancy and no infection
topics.corePiece: Saline infusion sonohysterography (SIS) distends the endometrial cavity with sterile saline introduced through a thin catheter during transvaginal imaging, outlining the endometrium. Indications include abnormal uterine bleeding, a thickened or poorly seen endometrium, suspected polyps or submucosal fibroids, infertility, suspected adhesions, and evaluation of congenital anomalies. It is ideally performed in the early proliferative phase, after menstrual bleeding stops and before ovulation, about days 5 to 10, when the endometrium is thinnest and an early pregnancy is not at risk. Contraindications include pregnancy and active pelvic infection or PID; unexplained pelvic tenderness should also delay the study. Flush the catheter with saline beforehand, because air bubbles can mimic polyps. A polyp appears as an echogenic intracavitary mass covered by endometrium, a submucosal fibroid as a hypoechoic broad-based mass beneath the endometrium, hyperplasia as diffuse thickening, and adhesions (Asherman syndrome) as echogenic bands bridging the cavity. A balloon catheter in the lower segment can hide lesions there, so deflate it at the end. Agitated saline can assess tubal patency (sonosalpingography).
topics.whyLock: Timing and contraindications are the most tested points. Scheduling in the early proliferative phase avoids disrupting a possible early pregnancy and gives the thinnest lining, so small polyps stand out. A trap is calling air bubbles polyps; bubbles are very bright, may shadow and move. Another is mistaking blood clot for a lesion; clot moves and lacks flow. Always look at the lower segment and cervix after deflating the balloon, because the balloon itself can hide lesions there.

topics.title: Amniocentesis & CVS
topics.frontClue: Amnio from 15 weeks in a cord-free pocket; CVS at 10 to 13 weeks
topics.corePiece: Amniocentesis samples amniotic fluid under continuous ultrasound guidance, usually from 15 weeks onward. Before the procedure, confirm fetal cardiac activity, gestational age, number of fetuses, placental location and a suitable pocket. Choose a pocket free of cord and fetal parts, ideally avoiding the placenta, and keep the needle tip in view. Early amniocentesis before 15 weeks increases pregnancy loss and clubfoot and is avoided. The procedure-related loss rate is low, often quoted at about 0.1 to 0.3 percent. Amniotic fluid can be tested for karyotype and microarray, infection and AFP with acetylcholinesterase for open neural tube defects. Chorionic villus sampling (CVS) obtains placental villi at about 10 to 13 weeks by a transcervical or transabdominal route, targeting the chorion frondosum. CVS before about 10 weeks is linked with limb reduction defects; confined placental mosaicism, in about 1 to 2 percent, may require amniocentesis to clarify; and CVS cannot assess AFP. After either procedure, document fetal heart activity, and give Rh-negative unsensitized patients Rh immune globulin.
topics.whyLock: Remember what each test samples: amniocentesis samples fetal cells and fluid, while CVS samples placenta, which explains mosaicism and the absence of AFP testing with CVS. The sonographer's role is planning and guidance: choose the pocket, track the needle tip, and confirm heart activity before and after. A trap is choosing the largest pocket even when the cord lies within it; color Doppler should confirm no cord in the path. Remember the Rh immune globulin step for Rh-negative patients.

topics.title: Safety, ALARA & Transvaginal Technique
topics.frontClue: Lowest output, shortest time, TIS early and TIB later, a clean covered probe
topics.corePiece: No confirmed harmful bioeffects of diagnostic ultrasound have been shown in the human fetus, but ultrasound deposits energy, so the ALARA principle (as low as reasonably achievable) applies: scan only when medically indicated, use the lowest output and shortest time that answers the question, and prefer receiver gain over transmit power. Monitor the on-screen thermal index (TI), the estimate of tissue heating, and mechanical index (MI), the estimate of cavitation risk. In the first trimester, before significant bone ossification, the soft tissue thermal index (TIS) is used; from about 10 weeks, when fetal bone is present, the bone thermal index (TIB) is more relevant. Spectral and color Doppler produce higher exposure than gray-scale imaging, so in early pregnancy cardiac activity is documented with M-mode. Transvaginal scanning requires an empty bladder, an explanation of the exam and consent, a chaperone according to policy, a probe cover (non-latex for latex allergy) and high-level disinfection between patients. A full bladder helps transabdominal pelvic imaging by displacing bowel.
topics.whyLock: The exam tests which index applies when and the practical steps of ALARA. Raising receiver gain improves brightness without increasing exposure, so it is the first choice; increasing output power is not. Doppler on an embryo is the classic wrong answer for documenting heart rate. For transvaginal scanning, the most tested points are bladder status, probe cover and high-level disinfection, since a probe cover can tear. A trap is filling the bladder before a transvaginal scan; it pushes the pelvic organs out of the near field.
